note: Curated overview for awareness only. Acts and Articles are cited by name; section numbers are limited to ones widely published. Always confirm the current text on India Code (indiacode.nic.in) and consult a qualified advocate.

categories.title: Fundamental Rights
categories.summary: Basic rights guaranteed to every person in India by Part III of the Constitution. Most can be enforced directly in the Supreme Court (Article 32) or a High Court (Article 226).

rights.title: Right to Equality (Articles 14-18)
rights.explanation: The State must treat everyone equally before the law. Discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth is prohibited (Article 15), and there is equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16). Untouchability is abolished (Article 17).

rights.title: Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22)
rights.explanation: Includes freedom of speech and expression, peaceful assembly, forming associations, movement, residence and practising a profession (Article 19), subject to reasonable restrictions. Article 20 protects against retrospective punishment and self-incrimination. Article 21 protects life and personal liberty. Article 22 gives safeguards on arrest: to be told the grounds, to consult a lawyer, and to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

rights.title: Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24)
rights.explanation: Forced labour and human trafficking are prohibited. Children below 14 cannot be employed in factories, mines or other hazardous work.

rights.title: Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28)
rights.explanation: Every person may freely profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health.

rights.title: Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30)
rights.explanation: Minorities can protect their language, script and culture, and set up educational institutions of their choice.

rights.title: Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32)
rights.explanation: You can go directly to the Supreme Court if a fundamental right is violated. High Courts can be approached under Article 226.

rights.title: Right to Education (Article 21A)
rights.explanation: Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14.

references.label: Article 21A
references.note: Right to education, inserted by the 86th Amendment

categories.title: Consumer Rights
categories.summary: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 protects buyers of goods and services, including online shoppers, against defective goods, deficient services and unfair trade practices.

rights.title: Right to Safety, Information and Choice
rights.explanation: You have the right to be protected from hazardous goods, to know quality, quantity, price and ingredients, and to choose among competing products.

rights.title: Right to be Heard and to Seek Redressal
rights.explanation: You can file a complaint before the District, State or National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission depending on the value of the claim.

rights.title: Product liability and unfair trade practices
rights.explanation: Manufacturers, sellers and service providers can be held liable for harm from defective products or services. Misleading advertisements can be acted on by the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA).

rights.title: E-commerce protection
rights.explanation: Online sellers and platforms have duties under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, including displaying seller details and handling grievances.

rights.title: Online complaints
rights.explanation: Complaints can be filed online through the e-Daakhil portal. The National Consumer Helpline (1915) offers pre-litigation help.

categories.title: Women's Rights
categories.summary: Indian law provides specific protection against domestic violence, workplace sexual harassment, dowry demands and sexual offences, along with maintenance and maternity rights.

rights.title: Protection from domestic violence
rights.explanation: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 covers physical, emotional, sexual and economic abuse. A woman can seek protection orders, residence orders and monetary relief through a Magistrate, with help from a Protection Officer.

rights.title: Cruelty by husband or relatives
rights.explanation: Cruelty to a married woman by her husband or his relatives, including harassment for dowry, is a criminal offence (Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 498A of the IPC). The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 also applies.

rights.title: Safe workplace
rights.explanation: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 requires employers with 10 or more employees to set up an Internal Committee to hear complaints.

rights.title: Zero FIR and free legal aid
rights.explanation: A complaint of a serious offence can be registered at any police station irrespective of where it happened, and it is then transferred. Women are entitled to free legal services through legal services authorities.

rights.title: Maternity benefits
rights.explanation: Under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (as amended in 2017) eligible women employees get paid maternity leave of 26 weeks for the first two children.

rights.title: Stalking and sexual harassment
rights.explanation: Stalking (Section 78 BNS) and sexual harassment (Section 75 BNS) are punishable offences.

references.label: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 - Sections 75, 78, 85
references.note: Verify current text on India Code

sources.name: Ministry of Women and Child Development

categories.title: Cybercrime Awareness
categories.summary: Online fraud, identity theft, harassment and privacy violations are covered by the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

rights.title: Report quickly
rights.explanation: For online financial fraud, call 1930 immediately; the faster you report, the better the chance of freezing the money. You can also file a complaint at the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

rights.title: Identity theft and cheating by personation
rights.explanation: Sections 66C and 66D of the IT Act, 2000 punish using someone's password or identity and cheating by impersonation using a computer resource.

rights.title: Privacy violations
rights.explanation: Section 66E of the IT Act punishes capturing or publishing private images without consent. Section 67 deals with publishing obscene material electronically.

rights.title: Cheating
rights.explanation: Online cheating can also be prosecuted as cheating under Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

rights.title: Personal data
rights.explanation: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 gives individuals rights over their personal data, such as access, correction and grievance redressal, and places duties on organisations that process it. Check which provisions are in force.

rights.title: Keep evidence
rights.explanation: Save screenshots, transaction IDs, URLs, phone numbers and messages. Do not delete chats. Never share OTPs, PINs or passwords.

references.label: Information Technology Act, 2000 - Sections 66C, 66D, 66E, 67
references.note: Verify current text on India Code

categories.title: Labour Rights
categories.summary: Workers are protected on wages, working conditions, social security and dismissal. India has consolidated many older laws into four Labour Codes.

rights.title: Timely and minimum wages
rights.explanation: Employers must pay at least the applicable minimum wage and pay on time. Unlawful deductions are not allowed. These rules are now in the Code on Wages, 2019.

rights.title: Provident fund, ESI and gratuity
rights.explanation: Eligible employees get provident fund, health insurance through ESIC and gratuity after the qualifying service period, now covered by the Code on Social Security, 2020.

rights.title: Safe working conditions
rights.explanation: Employers must provide a safe workplace, with limits on working hours and overtime pay, under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.

rights.title: Industrial disputes and dismissal
rights.explanation: Rules on layoffs, retrenchment and raising a dispute are in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020. Workers can approach the labour authorities or conciliation officer.

rights.title: Check commencement
rights.explanation: The four Labour Codes replace many older Acts. Check the Ministry of Labour and Employment for which provisions and state rules currently apply.

references.label: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020

categories.title: Tenant Rights
categories.summary: Rental rules in India are mainly state laws. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is a central template that states may adopt, so your rights depend on your state.

rights.title: Written agreement
rights.explanation: Always have a written rent or lease agreement. A lease of immovable property for more than one year must be registered (Registration Act, 1908; Transfer of Property Act, 1882). Many people use an 11-month agreement, but the rules and stamp duty vary by state.

rights.title: No arbitrary eviction
rights.explanation: A landlord generally cannot throw a tenant out without following legal procedure and valid grounds under the applicable state rent law. Cutting off water or electricity to force a tenant out is not permitted.

rights.title: Security deposit
rights.explanation: The deposit should be refunded after deducting only lawful dues. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 proposes limits on deposits, but it applies only where your state has adopted it.

rights.title: Notice and rent increase
rights.explanation: Rent changes and termination usually require notice as per the agreement and state law.

rights.title: Keep records
rights.explanation: Pay by bank transfer, ask for receipts and keep photos of the property condition at move-in.

references.label: Model Tenancy Act, 2021
references.note: Central model law; applies only if adopted by the state

sources.name: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

categories.title: New Criminal Laws (BNS, BNSS, BSA)
categories.summary: From 1 July 2024, three new laws replaced the colonial-era criminal laws: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the IPC, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replaced the CrPC, and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) replaced the Indian Evidence Act.

rights.title: BNS replaces the IPC
rights.explanation: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines offences and punishments. Examples: murder (Section 103), theft (Section 303), cheating (Section 318). Old IPC section numbers have changed, so check the BNS number for offences from 1 July 2024 onwards.

rights.title: BNSS replaces the CrPC
rights.explanation: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 governs procedure: FIR, arrest, bail, investigation and trial. It also allows electronic reporting of offences and recognises Zero FIR.

rights.title: BSA replaces the Evidence Act
rights.explanation: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 governs what counts as evidence, and expressly recognises electronic records.

rights.title: Your rights on arrest
rights.explanation: You must be told the grounds of arrest, can inform a relative or friend, can consult a lawyer, and must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Article 22 of the Constitution).

rights.title: Offences before 1 July 2024
rights.explanation: Offences committed before that date are generally still dealt with under the old laws. Ask a lawyer which law applies to your case.
